title: Antigen-chosen pharmacological control of immune memory

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an administered pharmacological treatment that durably changes the immune response to a chosen antigen while preserving useful responses to unrelated antigens. Its tolerance component would teach the immune system to stop attacking a particular target associated with disease. The broader ambition also includes reversing that tolerance when needed or deliberately establishing a chosen protective response. These are distinct capabilities; demonstrating one would not establish the others.

A concrete starting point is KAN-101, an investigational product that combines a gliadin peptide with a liver-targeting glycosylation signature and is designed to induce immune tolerance to gliadin in coeliac disease. This illustrates how an administered product could present a selected antigen in a setting intended to promote tolerance. The supplied human study establishes an early clinical investigation of that approach, rather than achievement of durable immune-memory control.

Conceptual clarification: controlling an antigen-specific response does not necessarily mean deleting the cells that remember it. Durable tolerance, selective erasure of memory, and reversible suppression of a response could produce different biological states. Likewise, protective priming substantially overlaps with vaccination. The distinctive ambition here is precise, durable and potentially reversible pharmacological control, whose individual components would each need demonstration.

significance.text: Conditional significance: durable tolerance to a pathogenic antigen, with unrelated protective responses retained, could let clinicians treat the immune response responsible for disease while reducing dependence on broad immunosuppression in suitable patients. The direct advance would be antigen-level selectivity combined with lasting clinical benefit. That combination could change treatment from repeated suppression of disease activity to sustained control after a finite treatment course.

Conditional downstream possibilities include treatment of selected autoimmune diseases, allergies and transplant-related immune responses. These applications would require separate evidence: the relevant antigen or antigens must be identifiable and addressable, the pathogenic response must remain controlled, and protection against infection and cancer must be assessed. A result against one known antigen would not establish that the same approach can accommodate the antigenic complexity of every disease or replace existing treatment across these fields.

The analogy to editing immune memory is useful only as a description of the intended selectivity. It should not imply that tolerance physically erases memory, that an established response can be switched back on at will, or that every patient's immune history can be rewritten predictably. Adding protective responses would also need a clearly defined advantage over existing vaccination. None of these broader capabilities is established by the supplied KAN-101 tolerance study.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unresolved capability within this record is durable clinical control of a chosen pathogenic immune response in humans, achieved pharmacologically while preserving unrelated protection. Reversibility and protective priming extend that objective and require additional evidence. The supplied abstract does not establish these outcomes, but its limited scope also cannot establish that they are absent everywhere in pharmacology.

Engineering synthesis: the challenge extends beyond temporarily inhibiting an inflammatory signal. An antigen-directed treatment must reach the appropriate biological setting, expose the relevant antigen in a way that reliably promotes the intended response, and maintain that response after treatment ends. The earlier description of tolerance as a cellular program usefully emphasizes this persistence problem, but the supplied abstract does not independently establish that mechanistic account or identify which cellular processes limit success.

Further proposed barriers are selecting the disease-driving antigen or antigen set, choosing an effective dose and delivery schedule, avoiding unintended activation of the targeted response, and distinguishing lasting tolerance from a transient change in a biomarker. Selectivity also has to be demonstrated independently: improvement in the target disease does not by itself show that unrelated immunity remains intact.

For the broader ambition, reversibility would require a dependable way to restore an appropriate response after tolerance has been induced. Selective memory erasure would require evidence that distinguishes loss of memory from continued regulation of an existing response. Protective priming would require a defined capability beyond ordinary vaccine-induced immunity. These are separate scientific objectives rather than automatic consequences of successful antigen-specific tolerance.

current_state.text: The supplied human evidence is the completed first-in-human ACeD phase 1 study of KAN-101 in coeliac disease, reported by Murray and colleagues in 2023 and published in the August 2023 issue of The Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology. KAN-101 contains a gliadin peptide conjugated to a liver-targeting glycosylation signature and was designed to induce tolerance to gliadin. The primary endpoint was the incidence and severity of adverse events.

The authors reported an acceptable safety profile. The abstract described future evaluation of safety and efficacy, including biomarker responses during a gluten challenge, at doses of 0.6 mg/kg and greater. That dose statement concerns planned evaluation; it is not an established effective-dose threshold. The supplied abstract does not establish durable clinical remission, reversibility, selective memory erasure, protective priming or preserved unrelated protective immunity.

The abstract stated that coeliac disease had no approved therapies at the time of the report. This is a historical statement from the 2023 publication. The review inspected only the PubMed abstract and bibliographic record, not the full article or its detailed analyses. Although the saved record was retrieved on November 1, 2026, later publications, efficacy outcomes and trial-registry updates were not checked, and no freshness search was supplied. The dated study therefore cannot establish the field's status on that later date; the access limitation does not invalidate its reported early safety findings.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration for the tolerance component: controlled human trials in at least two unrelated immune diseases with known relevant antigens should show durable clinical remission after the pharmacological treatment course, off broad immunosuppression, together with retained responses to an unrelated vaccine or infectious antigen. The two-disease threshold is an author-selected test of breadth, not an established standard. Successful finite trials would demonstrate benefit within their studied diseases and populations, rather than universal antigen-level control.
completion_criteria.label: Selective durable remission off broad immunosuppression in two unrelated diseases

completion_criteria.text: Proposed trial requirements: prespecify the duration that counts as durable, permitted background treatment, clinically meaningful remission endpoints, disease-relevant exposure or challenge conditions, and measures of retained protective responses. Follow-up should establish whether benefit persists after dosing ends and document relapse, retreatment and adverse outcomes. Responses to a limited set of unrelated antigens would support selectivity within those tests; they would not prove preservation of all immunity against infection or cancer.
completion_criteria.label: Prespecified durability criteria and follow-up document sustained benefit and harms

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: confirm the result in independent cohorts or trials, characterize which patients and antigen profiles respond, and establish a reproducible product, dose and administration schedule. A safety study or a short-lived biomarker change after antigen challenge would not by itself demonstrate durable clinical tolerance. An engineered cell therapy manufactured outside the body would also fall outside this record's chosen pharmacological scope, even if it produced a related immune effect.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication establishes responders and reproducible pharmacological treatment

completion_criteria.text: Separate proposed demonstrations are needed for the broader claims. Reversibility should require restoration of an appropriate antigen-specific response after induced tolerance, with acceptable safety and prespecified clinical or functional evidence. A claim of selective memory erasure would require evidence distinguishing erasure from ongoing regulation. Protective priming should demonstrate a clinically useful protective response and specify the additional control offered beyond existing vaccination. Passing the tolerance benchmark alone would not complete these other components.
completion_criteria.label: Distinct evidence establishes reversibility, selective memory erasure and protective priming

related_concepts.text: Roster comparison — PHA-03, General prevention of idiosyncratic immune-mediated drug injury: both concern avoiding harmful immune responses. PHA-04 focuses on controlling a selected antigen-specific response; PHA-03 concerns general prevention of immune injury caused by drugs. An antigen-directed tolerance approach might help with particular drug-associated responses if their relevant targets were known, but that would not establish general prevention of idiosyncratic injury.

Roster comparison — PHA-02, Prospective prediction of human efficacy, dose, and major toxicity before first-in-human exposure: better prediction could assist development of antigen-directed products, but prediction and therapeutic control are separate achievements. PHA-04 requires demonstrated clinical efficacy, durability and selectivity even if a predictive method successfully forecasts them.

Roster comparison — PHA-06, In-place pharmacological replacement of missing human cell types: both envision administered products producing lasting changes in biological function. PHA-04 seeks to redirect an immune response and does not require replacement of a missing cell type. Its exclusion of externally manufactured cell therapy is a scope choice, not evidence that it accomplishes cell replacement.

Roster comparison — PHA-05, Systemic pharmacological access to brain parenchyma for arbitrary drug classes, and PHA-11, Reliable oral systemic exposure for folded peptides and proteins: delivery can constrain antigen-directed treatment, but these entries address different delivery barriers. Liver-targeted delivery in the KAN-101 example does not establish general brain access or reliable oral exposure. Conversely, solving either delivery problem would not by itself establish antigen-specific tolerance.

Roster comparison — PHA-13, A medicine that holds its own therapeutic window without an external controller: a durable immune effect and autonomous control of drug exposure are distinct properties. PHA-04 would still require appropriate dosing and safety monitoring; lasting tolerance does not imply that a medicine regulates its own therapeutic window.

Roster comparison — PHA-08, Anti-infective drugs that eradicate dormant persisters without seeding genetic resistance: preserving protective immunity during antigen-directed treatment is relevant to infection risk, but it is different from eliminating persistent pathogens. Neither achievement would establish the other. These relationships leave the supplied roster entries distinct.

change_log.reason: The broader concept remains useful, but the supplied tolerance study does not establish these capabilities as a single achieved package.

change_log.change: Replaced categorical claims about what pharmacology cannot do with a defined proposed capability and bounded evidence statements.
change_log.reason: One phase 1 abstract cannot establish a field-wide absence of selective immune-memory control.

change_log.change: Retained the cellular-program explanation as explicitly labeled engineering synthesis and expanded the concrete development barriers.
change_log.reason: It helps explain the persistence challenge, but the supplied abstract does not substantiate a general mechanistic account.

change_log.change: Made the significance conditional and distinguished antigen-level selectivity from replacement of broad immunosuppression across whole disease categories.
change_log.reason: Clinical applicability depends on disease-specific antigens, durable benefit and retained protective immunity.

change_log.change: Specified the 2023 trial's safety endpoint and preserved the planned evaluation at doses of 0.6 mg/kg and greater.
change_log.reason: These details clarify demonstrated scope without presenting a future efficacy evaluation as an achieved result.

change_log.change: Confined the approval statement to its historical context and preserved abstract-only access and missing freshness checks.
change_log.reason: Retrieval in 2026 does not make a 2023 report a verified account of current treatment availability or later trial outcomes.

change_log.change: Limited the original two-disease completion proposal to tolerance and added separate proposals for reversibility, erasure and priming.
change_log.reason: The original benchmark did not test the full concept, and its thresholds are proposals rather than established standards.

change_log.reason: Finite demonstrations establish studied breadth and selectivity, while adjacent pharmacological capabilities remain separate innovations.

unresolved_issues: Later KAN-101 efficacy results, registry updates and the field's status on November 1, 2026 remain unassessed.
The full trial article and detailed efficacy analyses were not inspected; conclusions are limited to the supplied abstract and bibliographic record.
The supplied evidence does not resolve whether KAN-101 produces durable remission or preserves unrelated protective immunity.
The cellular mechanisms necessary for durable, reversible control and the principal barriers across different diseases are not established by this source.
The novelty of protective priming beyond existing vaccination still requires a specific definition.
Durability periods, remission endpoints, acceptable background treatment and the breadth of protective-immunity testing remain to be specified for any actual completion trial.
No substantive review recommendation was rejected; mechanistic explanation was retained only as labeled synthesis rather than a source-established finding.

brief.title: Medicines that reshape immunity to a chosen target
possible: People whose immune systems attack a disease-related target could receive a finite course of medicine that stops that attack for the long term, while keeping useful responses to other targets.
The broader goal includes restoring a response after deliberately quieting it, or establishing a chosen protective response. Each capability would need its own demonstration.
why: For people with suitable autoimmune diseases, allergies or transplant-related immune reactions, lasting control could reduce dependence on medicines that broadly suppress immunity. Treatment could move from repeatedly suppressing disease activity to sustained benefit after dosing ends.

sources.showed: An early human trial found an acceptable safety profile for KAN-101, a medicine designed to quiet the response to a gluten component in coeliac disease. Treatment-related side effects were mild to moderate.
sources.quote: Rapid systemic clearance of KAN-101 was observed and no accumulation on repeated dosing.
sources.cited_for: This supports the feasibility of administering a medicine designed to quiet a chosen immune response.
sources.not_established: The trial did not establish lasting remission or preservation of unrelated protective responses.

sources.who: Stacie M Jones and colleagues for the Immune Tolerance Network
sources.showed: Giving peanut by mouth as treatment produced remission in some young children after treatment stopped. Younger children were more likely to reach remission. Dosing reactions were common.
sources.quote:
By use of multivariable regression analysis of participants receiving peanut oral immunotherapy, 
younger age and lower baseline peanut-specific IgE was predictive of remission.
sources.cited_for: This demonstrates that a chosen allergic response can remain quiet after treatment ends in some patients.
sources.not_established: Remission after a limited avoidance period does not establish permanent tolerance or preserved protection against unrelated targets.

sources.who: Ciarán P. Kelly, Joseph A. Murray and the TAK-101 Study Group
sources.showed: In a small, short trial, TAK-101 reduced gluten-triggered immune activation in people with coeliac disease. It packages a gluten component inside tiny particles.
sources.cited_for: This supports selectively reducing the immune response to a disease-related target in humans.
sources.not_established: The study did not establish lasting symptom control or broad preservation of protective immunity.

sources.showed: In adults with recently diagnosed diabetes caused by immune attack on insulin-producing cells, injections of a fragment of an insulin precursor were well tolerated. Daily insulin use remained unchanged in treated groups but rose with placebo.
sources.quote:
Treatment was well tolerated with  
no systemic or local hypersensitivity.
sources.cited_for: This provides early human evidence of treatment directed at a disease-related immune target beyond coeliac disease.
sources.not_established: The findings do not establish lasting remission after treatment or preservation of unrelated protective responses.

shown: The Immune Tolerance Network demonstrated peanut-allergy remission in some young children after treatment stopped, lasting through a 26-week avoidance period. This is evidence of benefit beyond dosing, though its longer duration remains unknown.

The TAK-101 Study Group reduced gluten-triggered immune activation in a small coeliac disease trial. Murray and colleagues established early safety findings for KAN-101. Neither result establishes lasting clinical remission with unrelated immunity preserved.
missing: Controlled human trials have yet to establish the combined goal of lasting disease remission after dosing and retained unrelated protective responses.
Independent studies must establish which patients respond and a reproducible medicine, dose and treatment schedule.
Restoring a quieted response, selectively erasing immune memory and adding protection beyond vaccination each need separate demonstrations.

milestones.label: Lasting selective remission across two unrelated diseases
milestones.explanation: Controlled trials would have to show lasting remission after treatment in two unrelated diseases with known targets, without broad immune suppression and with unrelated protection retained. This would establish breadth and selectivity.

milestones.label: Defined follow-up establishes lasting benefit and harms
milestones.explanation: Trials would have to define lasting remission, allowed treatment, relevant exposures and protective-response tests, then track relapse, retreatment and harms after dosing. This would distinguish sustained benefit from temporary improvement.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce treatment and identify responders
milestones.explanation: Independent trials would have to reproduce benefits, identify responding patients and targets, and establish a consistent medicine, dose and schedule. This would define reliable treatment and its practical boundaries.

milestones.label: Restoration, memory erasure and added protection receive distinct proof
milestones.explanation: Separate studies would have to safely restore responses, distinguish memory erasure from continued restraint, and establish useful protection with added control beyond vaccination. Successful tolerance alone would not establish these abilities.

uncertain: How long must remission last, and under what exposures and background treatment, to count as durable?
How broadly must unrelated immune responses be tested to establish retained protection?
What additional control would establishing a protective response offer beyond existing vaccination?

page.title: Pharmacological induction of antigen-specific immune tolerance
page.definition: An administered medicine establishes disease control that persists after treatment ends by selectively quieting responses to a chosen antigen, a molecular target recognised by the immune system, while preserving protective responses to unrelated antigens. A Timothy grass pollen tablet illustrates the clinical part of this goal. After three years of daily treatment, adults had lower combined symptom and medication scores than placebo recipients during their first pollen season off treatment.

goal.need: About 1 in 120 people worldwide have biopsy-confirmed coeliac disease. In a ten-day study, 12 of 18 adults following a gluten-free diet were exposed to gluten, usually without knowing it. Lasting tolerance could protect the small intestine when food is contaminated. Eating ordinary portions of gluten safely would require protection at higher exposures. For patients who need broad immunosuppression to control autoimmune disease or prevent graft rejection, a selective treatment could preserve their ability to fight infections.

figures.caption: Peanut-allergy remission after treatment withdrawal in IMPACT, published in 2022
figures.note: Participants were aged 12 to younger than 48 months. Remission required passing a double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge with 5000 mg peanut protein.

statements.quote: Antigen-specific tolerance induction is a major goal for the treatment or prevention of autoimmune disease and graft rejection
Immune tolerance-inducing therapies reprogramme immune cells to eliminate pathogenic immune responses while preserving protective immunity.

completion.title: An antigen-directed medicine induces off-treatment tolerance while preserving protective immunity.
completion.criterion: Following an administered antigen-directed treatment, humans show selective elimination of pathogenic immune responses to the relevant antigens while preserving protective immunity, without ongoing treatment with the tolerance-inducing intervention. NIAID's definition specifies no minimum follow-up duration, responder fraction or protective-antigen panel. The clinical and immunological components must coexist; a target biomarker change or remission over one withdrawal interval alone does not establish the combined phenotype.
completion.set_by: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, RFA-AI-12-043, Section I, 'Purpose' (2012 definition of immune tolerance).
completion.threshold_quote: while preserving protective immunity and does not require ongoing treatment with the intervention.
completion.basis: This published programme definition contains the three components of the capability: antigen selectivity, protective immunity and persistence without continued intervention. It provides a functional criterion rather than a numerical validation protocol. IMPACT establishes remission through a defined withdrawal interval; TAK-101 establishes a target-specific immune effect. Neither result alone establishes the complete phenotype.

milestones.title: An antigen-directed treatment reduces an animal's response to its target in a controlled challenge.
milestones.criterion: Challenge treated and control animals with the same target antigen. The treated group must show a lower target-specific antibody or T-cell response than the control group. The experimental oral-tolerance convention specifies no minimum effect size.
milestones.set_by: Experimental oral-tolerance convention described in Janeway's Immunobiology, tenth edition; the textbook's worked example uses ovalbumin in mice.
milestones.threshold_quote: Mice that were fed ovalbumin have a lower ovalbumin-specific systemic immune response than that of mice fed the control protein.

milestones.title: An antigen-directed investigational medicine is administered to people in a phase 1 study.
milestones.criterion: Administer the investigational antigen-directed medicine to people in a phase 1 study that evaluates its pharmacological effects and monitors adverse effects.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Drug Development and Review Definitions, 'Phase I Clinical Studies'.
milestones.threshold_quote: Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans.

milestones.title: An antigen-directed medicine reduces its target response in a controlled human antigen-challenge study.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate a smaller target-specific immune response after antigen challenge in treated participants than in controls, using the study's prespecified endpoint. In the TAK-101 coeliac protocol, compare the change from baseline to gluten-challenge day 6 in the number of gliadin-responsive, interferon-γ-producing cells per million peripheral blood mononuclear cells.
milestones.set_by: TAK-101 Study Group, registered phase 2a study NCT03738475; assay and challenge particulars were published for coeliac disease.
milestones.threshold_quote: gluten-stimulated IFN-γ production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) on day 6 of gluten challenge

milestones.title: An antigen-directed medicine produces clinical remission after treatment withdrawal.
milestones.criterion: Meet a prespecified clinical remission endpoint after withdrawing the tolerance-inducing treatment. In IMPACT, children aged 12 to under 48 months at enrolment stop dosing after 134 weeks and avoid dietary peanut for 26 weeks. At week 160, compare the proportions in the immunotherapy and placebo groups who pass a double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge with a cumulative 5000 mg of peanut protein. The withdrawal interval and challenge dose apply to this protocol.
milestones.set_by: Immune Tolerance Network, IMPACT study NCT03345160; its numerical remission endpoint is specific to peanut allergy.
milestones.threshold_quote: remission, defined as passing the 5000 mg DBPCFC 26 weeks after oral immunotherapy discontinuation;

milestones.title: An antigen-directed medicine meets a prespecified clinical efficacy endpoint during treatment.
milestones.criterion: Meet the disease protocol's clinical endpoint during treatment. In IMPACT, children aged 12 to under 48 months at enrolment undergo a double-blind, placebo-controlled food challenge at the end of 134 weeks of dosing. Compare the proportions in the immunotherapy and placebo groups who tolerate a cumulative 5000 mg of peanut protein. The dose and timing apply to the peanut protocol.
milestones.set_by: Immune Tolerance Network, IMPACT study NCT03345160, primary desensitisation endpoint.
milestones.threshold_quote: desensitised after 134 weeks of oral immunotherapy, defined as passing the 5000 mg peanut DBPCFC.

not_found: No universal duration or protective-immunity assay threshold for antigen-specific immune tolerance was found.
No common numerical definition of off-treatment remission was found for coeliac disease, peanut allergy and type 1 diabetes.

results.finding: In the 41-participant phase 1 coeliac disease trial, 35 adults received intravenous KAN-101.
results.detail: Part A evaluated single ascending doses. Part B evaluated multiple ascending doses against placebo.
results.quote: 14 patients were assigned to part A (four 0·15 mg/kg, three 0·3 mg/kg, three 0·6 mg/kg, three 1·2 mg/kg, one 1·5 mg/kg) and 27 patients to part B (six 0·15 mg/kg with two placebo, seven 0·3 mg/kg with two placebo, and eight 0·6 mg/kg with two placebo).

results.finding: In 146 children with peanut allergy, oral immunotherapy increased week-134 desensitisation by 69 percentage points versus placebo.
results.detail: The primary analysis counted missing challenges as failures. The per-protocol comparison also favored immunotherapy.
results.quote:
Assessment of desensitisation at week 134 showed that 
68 (71%, 95% CI 61–80) of 96 participants who received 
peanut oral immunotherapy passed the 5000 mg 
DPBCFC compared with one (2%, 0·05–11) of 50 who 
received placebo (risk difference [RD] 69%, 95% CI 
59–79; p<0·0001; figure 2A).

results.finding: In 146 children with peanut allergy, oral immunotherapy increased week-160 remission by 19 percentage points versus placebo.
results.detail: The trial counted missing challenges as failures. The per-protocol comparison also favored immunotherapy, despite greater dropout in the placebo group.

peanut oral immunotherapy passed the 5000 mg

results.finding: In a trial of 146 children with peanut allergy, oral immunotherapy reduced ex vivo basophil activation to peanut at week 160.
results.detail: The paper describes the direction of the basophil effect in prose and refers to the appendix for the quantitative comparison.
results.quote:
Compared with placebo, peanut oral immunotherapy decreased peanut-specific and Ara h2-specific 
IgE, skin prick test, and basophil activation, and increased peanut-specific and Ara h2-specific IgG4 at weeks 134 
and 160.

results.finding: In a phase 1b proinsulin peptide trial in adults with new-onset type 1 diabetes (n=27), zero hypersensitivity reactions were reported.
results.detail: The trial monitored patients for at least one hour after each injection. Local erythema occurred in both peptide groups and in the placebo group.
results.quote:
Treatment was well tolerated with  
no systemic or local hypersensitivity.

results.finding: In adults with new-onset type 1 diabetes (n=27 randomized), high-frequency peptide dosing increased ex vivo proinsulin-stimulated IL-10 responses versus placebo (p=0.015).
results.detail: The significant result was an increase in a regulatory cytokine response. The treated-versus-placebo comparison did not establish suppression of the IFN-γ response.
results.quote:
Over the 
duration of the treatment period, cumulative CD4 T cell IL -10 responses to proinsulin 
stimulation were significantly higher in the blood of  the high frequency compared with placebo 
(p=0.015) and low frequency groups (p=0.003; Figure 4A ).

results.finding: In adults with new-onset type 1 diabetes (n=27 randomized), stimulated C-peptide fell less with high-frequency dosing than with placebo at month 3 (p=0.03).
results.detail: Safety was the primary endpoint. The phase 1b trial was designed to inform future studies and was underpowered for efficacy.
results.quote:
There was

results.finding: BALB/cJ mice had nearly undetectable Ara h 2–specific IgE and IgG1 after treatment (n = 5 per group for the anaphylaxis challenge).
results.detail: Figure 2 gives the per-group sample size for the anaphylaxis challenge. The antibody measurements were taken after the shared allergen boost, before the anaphylaxis challenge.
results.quote: levels were nearly undetectable in Ara h 2–specific mCD22L-STAL–treated mice and significantly lower compared to the immunogenic liposome–treated group.

results.finding: HHD II mice (n = 3 per group) given ZnT8-coupled beads showed lower ZnT8-specific CD8+ T-cell proliferation 5 days after challenge.
results.detail: Figure 3g used CFSE dilution to measure proliferation of transferred ZnT8-specific CD8+ T cells.
results.quote:
The
ZnT8-specific T cells isolated from both the spleen and lymph
nodes of the mice treated with ZnT8-PSB exhibited a signif-
icantly lower proliferative capacity than those from the control
mice (Fig. 3g).

results.finding: In a type 1 diabetes cohort (24 recruited), ZnT8-coupled beads suppressed CD8+ T-cell responses to 3 ZnT8 epitopes in vitro.
results.detail: The text gives the recruitment total but does not specify how many participants contributed cells to each epitope comparison.
results.quote:
Compared with those exposed to the control human
immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-PSB, CD8 + T cells co-
cultured with ZnT8-PSB displayed significantly diminished
responses to the re-stimulation with the ZnT8-3, ZnT8-6 and
ZnT8-9 epitopes (Fig. 8a–c).

results.finding: Among 18 children completing the peanut immunotherapy trial, symptoms were reported with 11.5% of active doses.
results.detail: Eleven children received active treatment and seven received placebo. Staff monitored observed dosing, and families recorded symptoms after home doses.
results.quote: Symptoms were reported with 11.5% of peanut doses and 8.6% of placebo doses

results.finding: In 18 children, the peanut skin-prick wheal was smaller with sublingual immunotherapy than with placebo (p=0.020).
results.detail: For each child, investigators followed the peanut extract dilution selected at baseline and subtracted the saline-control wheal size.
results.quote: After 12 months, SPT in the active treatment group was significantly smaller than in the placebo group [p=0.020] with a median wheal size of 4 mm (range 0 – 11 mm) in the active treatment group and 11.5 mm (range 3.5 – 21 mm) in the placebo group

results.finding: In 18 children, peanut sublingual immunotherapy increased the on-treatment food-challenge threshold versus placebo (p=0.011).
results.detail: The primary endpoint compared cumulative peanut protein ingested before symptoms required treatment and challenge discontinuation.
results.quote: The 11 subjects randomized to active peanut SLIT treatment safely ingested a median cumulative dose of 1710 mg of peanut protein compared to the 7 subjects on placebo who ingested a median cumulative dose of 85 mg [p=0.011].

results.finding: In the GAD-alum trial (n = 109), 49% of active-arm participants reported at least one adverse event.
results.detail: The safety set comprised 57 active-arm and 52 placebo-arm participants.
results.quote: The proportion of patients with any adverse event was 49% in the actively treated group and 58% in the placebo group

results.finding: In the GAD-alum trial (n = 109), GAD65-stimulated cell proliferation increased in treated HLA DR3-DQ2 carriers versus placebo.
results.detail: The supplied text reports the direction and significance of the proliferation result. It gives no numerical effect size or assay-specific sample size in prose.
results.quote:
but patients with HLA DR3-DQ2 had both significantly increased proliferation index (

) and significantly increased GAD-stimulated IL-10 and IL-13 compared with those negative for HLA DR3-DQ2 or patients in the placebo group

results.finding: In recent-onset type 1 diabetes (n = 108), the primary C-peptide endpoint was missed, with a GAD-alum versus placebo effect ratio of 1.091.
results.detail: GAD-alum injections ended on day 90 and vitamin D or its placebo ended on day 120. The subgroup analysis was added by protocol amendment before unblinding.

results.finding: Among HLA DR3-DQ2 carriers (n = 48 in the full analysis set), GAD-alum improved off-treatment partial remission (P = 0.0310).
results.detail: The Methods list IDAA1c ≥9 as a secondary endpoint. The Results define partial remission as IDAA1c ≤9.

1c

P
= 0.0310)

results.finding: In 23 adults with coeliac disease, phase 1 intravenous TAK-101 dosing reached 8 mg/kg.
results.detail: Two participants at the highest single dose had moderate infusion reactions. One discontinued treatment. The study reported no serious adverse events.
results.quote: TAK-101 was well tolerated at doses up to 8 mg/kg after single and repeated intravenous administrations 7 days apart.

results.finding: In 29 adults with coeliac disease, TAK-101 reduced the day-6 increase in gliadin-responsive IFN-γ spot-forming units by 88% versus placebo.
In the 28-adult coeliac histology threshold analysis, TAK-101 yielded a nonsignificant difference versus placebo (P = .1367).
results.detail: The threshold was a decline of at least 0.4 in the villus height-to-crypt depth ratio. It occurred in 3 of 13 TAK-101 recipients and 8 of 15 placebo recipients.
results.quote:
A decrease in Vh:Cd of at least 0.4 was measured in 8 (53.3%) of 15 patients in the placebo group and 3 (23.1%) of 13 patients treated with TAK-101, but this difference between the groups was not significant (
P
= .1367).

results.finding: Among 80 adults with type 1 diabetes randomized to BHT-3021 or placebo, zero serious adverse events were attributed to BHT-3021.
results.detail: The paper describes dose escalation and cohort expansion. The phase 1 designation remains unverified from the supplied text.
results.quote: No serious adverse events related to BHT-3021 occurred.

results.finding: In 24 adults with type 1 diabetes, week-15 changes in proinsulin-specific CD8 T-cell frequency favored BHT-3021 over placebo (P = 0.0142).
results.detail: The assay counted circulating antigen-specific cells. The mixed-meal test assessed endogenous insulin secretion.
results.quote:
For proinsulin HLA-A3–specific CD8

results.finding: In 38 adults with type 1 diabetes in the 1-mg and placebo comparison, mean stimulated C-peptide rose 19.5% from baseline in the treated group at week 15.
results.detail: The trial's primary objective was safety. HbA1c and insulin use did not differ significantly from placebo.

results.finding: In the 38-person comparison in type 1 diabetes, mean C-peptide was 19.5% above baseline in the 1-mg BHT-3021 arm after withdrawal.
results.detail: Participants continued insulin replacement. The paper reports no significant differences from placebo in insulin use or HbA1c.
results.quote: These data suggest that BHT-3021 may preserve β cell mass and/or function during the dosing period of 12 weeks and for up to 3 more months (6-month time point) after cessation of dosing. This effect is ultimately lost after discontinuation of therapy.

results.finding: In 23 adults who started injected insulin, prior nasal insulin reduced insulin antibodies versus placebo (P = 0.019).
results.detail: The separate proinsulin T-cell assay used ex vivo stimulation in five participants per arm during nasal treatment.

results.finding: In 52 adults, nasal insulin did not slow the decline in stimulated C-peptide versus placebo (P = 0.99 for the slope comparison).
results.detail: The slope comparison spans the study, including follow-up after the 12-month dosing period.
results.quote: The decline in β-cell function did not differ between the nasal insulin and placebo groups

results.finding: Among 23 adults with type 1 diabetes who started injected insulin, prior nasal insulin reduced the insulin antibody response versus placebo (P = 0.019).
results.detail: The proinsulin T-cell assay used ex vivo stimulation of blood cells from five participants per arm and therefore did not supply a controlled challenge in participants.
results.quote: After treatment with subcutaneous insulin, the induced IA response ( Table 2 ) was significantly blunted in participants who had received nasal insulin.

results.finding: In 52 adults with type 1 diabetes, nasal insulin did not slow the decline in stimulated C-peptide versus placebo (P = 0.99).
results.detail: The reported slope comparison spans the study, including the 12 months after dosing stopped.
results.quote: The decline in β-cell function did not differ between the nasal insulin and placebo groups ( Fig. 1 A  and  B ).

results.finding: In phase 1 studies of Nexvax2 in 82 adults with coeliac disease, the maximum tolerated intradermal dose was 150 µg.
results.detail: The maximum tolerated dose was established for twice-weekly dosing. The main pharmacodynamic endpoint was interferon-γ release in response to Nexvax2 peptides.
results.quote: The MTD for Nexvax2 was 150 µg due to transient, acute gastrointestinal adverse events with onset at 2 to 5 h after initial doses of Nexvax2, similar to those caused by gluten ingestion.

results.finding: In adults with grass pollen allergy (n=84 per protocol), two years of immunotherapy significantly reduced nasal Th2 cytokine responses to pollen challenge versus placebo.
results.detail: The article gives no numerical effect size in the prose for the individual nasal cytokine comparisons. Suppression was no longer evident one year after treatment ended.
results.quote: Nasal allergen challenge-induced increases in interleukin (IL)-4, IL-5 and IL-13 in nasal fluids were significantly suppressed after 2 years treatment with either subcutaneous or sublingual immunotherapy, as shown in

results.finding: Grass pollen allergic rhinitis (108 randomized): SLIT plus dupilumab reduced the early skin response by 19.9% versus double placebo one year after treatment ended.
results.detail: The early skin response was measured 15 minutes after intradermal grass pollen challenge. The abstract does not establish that this measure was the prespecified endpoint.
results.quote: At year 3, one year after completing two years of treatment, SLIT/dupilumab suppressed skin EPR by 19.9% compared to placebo (p<0.001), with significant suppression on LPR by 33.7% (p<0.001).

results.finding: In PPOIT-003 (201 children with peanut allergy), 51% of those assigned to peanut oral immunotherapy alone achieved sustained unresponsiveness.
results.quote: 36 (46%) of 79 children in the PPOIT group and 42 (51%) of 83 children in the OIT group achieved sustained unresponsiveness compared with two (5%) of 39 children in the placebo group

results.finding: Grass pollen allergic rhinitis (108 randomized): combination therapy reduced nasal challenge symptom scores by 36.4% versus double placebo one year after withdrawal.
results.detail: The primary endpoint was the area under the total nasal symptom score curve during the first hour of grass pollen nasal challenge. The abstract reports a group-level reduction in symptoms and gives no participant-level remission result.
results.quote: At year 3, one year after completing two years of treatment, SLIT/dupilumab reduced NAC-TNSS by 36.4% compared to placebo (p<0.001), and significantly improved PNIF by 28.5% (p=0.004).

definition = "An administered medicine establishes disease control that persists after treatment ends by selectively quieting responses to a chosen antigen, a molecular target recognised by the immune system, while preserving protective responses to unrelated antigens. A Timothy grass pollen tablet illustrates the clinical part of this goal. After three years of daily treatment, adults had lower combined symptom and medication scores than placebo recipients during their first pollen season off treatment.". Reason: The definition gains a clinical example that shows what an existing medicine has achieved and what its endpoint measured.

goal.need = "About 1 in 120 people worldwide have biopsy-confirmed coeliac disease. In a ten-day study, 12 of 18 adults following a gluten-free diet were exposed to gluten, usually without knowing it. Lasting tolerance could protect the small intestine when food is contaminated. Eating ordinary portions of gluten safely would require protection at higher exposures. For patients who need broad immunosuppression to control autoimmune disease or prevent graft rejection, a selective treatment could preserve their ability to fight infections.". Reason: The revision distinguishes biopsy-confirmed prevalence from positive antibody tests and explains what lasting protection would change for patients.
add case "Grass pollen allergy". Reason: Grass pollen allergy supplies a controlled human withdrawal study with a clinical endpoint specific to seasonal allergic rhinitis.

edit m1: criterion = "Challenge treated and control animals with the same target antigen. The treated group must show a lower target-specific antibody or T-cell response than the control group. The experimental oral-tolerance convention specifies no minimum effect size."; threshold_quote = "Mice that were fed ovalbumin have a lower ovalbumin-specific systemic immune response than that of mice fed the control protein."; threshold_ref = 6. Reason: Mouse group sizes and published gliadin results obscure the comparison that defines the animal milestone.

edit m2: criterion = "Administer the investigational antigen-directed medicine to people in a phase 1 study that evaluates its pharmacological effects and monitors adverse effects."; threshold_quote = "Phase 1 includes the initial introduction of an investigational new drug into humans."; threshold_ref = 8. Reason: The enrolment counts and observed adverse events are study results, while the FDA milestone is initial human administration.

edit m3: criterion = "Demonstrate a smaller target-specific immune response after antigen challenge in treated participants than in controls, using the study's prespecified endpoint. In the TAK-101 coeliac protocol, compare the change from baseline to gluten-challenge day 6 in the number of gliadin-responsive, interferon-\u03b3-producing cells per million peripheral blood mononuclear cells."; threshold_quote = "gluten-stimulated IFN-\u03b3 production in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) on day 6 of gluten challenge"; threshold_ref = 1. Reason: The revised criterion isolates the prespecified immune endpoint from the observed effect size, secondary histology findings and control stimulation.

add milestone after m3: "An antigen-directed medicine meets a prespecified clinical efficacy endpoint during treatment.". Reason: The existing sequence skips clinical benefit during dosing, which IMPACT measured separately from immune markers and remission after withdrawal.

edit m4: criterion = "Meet a prespecified clinical remission endpoint after withdrawing the tolerance-inducing treatment. In IMPACT, children aged 12 to under 48 months at enrolment stop dosing after 134 weeks and avoid dietary peanut for 26 weeks. At week 160, compare the proportions in the immunotherapy and placebo groups who pass a double-blind, placebo-controlled challenge with a cumulative 5000 mg of peanut protein. The withdrawal interval and challenge dose apply to this protocol."; threshold_quote = "remission, defined as passing the 5000 mg DBPCFC 26 weeks after oral immunotherapy discontinuation;"; threshold_ref = 2. Reason: The remission criterion now specifies the withdrawal conditions and the group comparison without incorporating the trial verdict.
remove not found 4. Reason: Reversing tolerance or erasing immune memory is a different intervention from inducing control of a pathogenic response.
remove not found 3. Reason: The access note identifies no missing scientific finding, and the published ACeD abstract reports the primary safety endpoint.
remove not found 2. Reason: Both KAN-101 trials now have publicly reported results, so the earlier difficulty displaying the registry pages no longer identifies an evidence gap.
remove not found 0. Reason: The phrase “these three diseases” loses its referent when grass pollen allergy is added.

add not found: "No common numerical definition of off-treatment remission was found for coeliac disease, peanut allergy and type 1 diabetes.". Reason: Naming the diseases preserves the scope of the original search for a shared remission threshold.
